title: sync: map transferred issues old -> new instead of deleting blindly, so the destination isn't re-analyzed from scratch
description:
## Context

When an issue is transferred from repo A to repo B, GitHub assigns it a **new number** in B and it leaves A entirely. Two independent consequences follow, and #53 only addressed the first:

1. **The source row became a ghost.** Sync is upsert-only, so A's row froze at `state='OPEN'` forever and paired with its own transferred copy as a near-identical cross-repo duplicate — dedup would then propose closing the *live* issue as a duplicate of one that no longer exists. #53 fixed this by deleting vanished rows during full syncs.
2. **The destination is re-analyzed from scratch.** Nothing links B#N back to A#1, so the transferred issue arrives in the mirror looking brand new: fresh embedding, fresh classification, fresh dedup, fresh review-queue proposals. This is still unaddressed.

Point 2 is partly defensible — labels and priority appropriate in repo B may genuinely differ from repo A — but it repeats LLM spend and human review for work already done, and it throws away the knowledge that the two are the same issue.

## What makes this newly possible

While verifying #54 I confirmed empirically that GitHub's REST redirect for a transferred issue returns the **new location**, not just a 200:

```
$ gh api repos/rstudio/thematic/issues/145
  number: 3902
  repository_url: https://api.github.com/repos/rstudio/shiny
  html_url: https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/issues/3902
```

Confirmed independently: `rstudio/shiny#3902`'s timeline carries a `TRANSFERRED_EVENT` with `fromRepository = rstudio/thematic`. A second case, `thematic#44 -> rstudio/bslib#83`, behaves the same. Genuinely-deleted numbers (`thematic#133`–`#137`) return 404 instead.

So at the moment reconciliation decides to retire a row, it can know **exactly where the issue went** — for free, from the same request that confirms the retirement is safe.

## Proposal

Persist the mapping when reconciliation retires a transferred (as opposed to deleted) issue, then use it. Roughly, in increasing order of value:

- **Record it.** Keep `(old_repo, old_number) -> (new_repo, new_number)` somewhere durable, so the transfer is a known fact rather than an inference. This alone makes the retirement auditable — right now the only record that a row was deleted is a log line and a `retired` count.
- **Skip redundant analysis.** Carry the existing classification (and embedding, if the content hash is unchanged) forward to the destination, so a transferred issue is not re-embedded and re-classified for identical text.
- **Suppress the ghost pair by identity** rather than relying on the source row's absence — a more direct fix for the original bug than deletion is.
- **Auto-resolve Transfers worklist entries.** #53's Transfers tab requires a human to click *Mark transferred* because nothing could detect the move. With the mapping, a suggested transfer whose issue is observed arriving in the suggested destination can close itself out, and the manual control becomes a fallback rather than the mechanism.

## Design questions to settle first

- **Where does the mapping live?** A new table implies a schema migration, which #53 deliberately avoided. An append-only JSONL artifact under `.data/` may fit the existing state-bus model better, and is rebuildable.
- **Does the destination repo need to be in `config/repos.yaml`?** If an issue is transferred to an unmirrored repo, the mapping is still worth recording even though the destination will never be synced.
- **Should classification really transfer?** Priority and labels are repo-specific; the argument for re-analyzing is not obviously wrong. Possibly carry the embedding (content-derived, repo-agnostic) but re-classify.
- **What about chains?** A -> B -> C. The redirect follows to the final location, so the mapping should probably store the terminal destination rather than each hop.

## Dependency

Best done **after #54**, which introduces the per-candidate confirmation read this feature would piggyback on. Doing it first would mean building the read twice.

_Filed from verification work on #54, itself from review of #53._

title: cross-repo duplicates close as NOT_PLANNED rather than DUPLICATE — verify whether duplicateIssueId accepts a cross-repo target
description:
## Context

Same-repo duplicates get GitHub's **native** duplicate linkage: the executor closes them with `closeIssue(stateReason: DUPLICATE, duplicateIssueId: …)`, so the issue shows as a real duplicate of its canonical.

Cross-repo duplicates do not. `src/triage_verse/executor.py:195-201` falls back to a plain `not planned` close plus a differently-worded comment template (`config/templates/close-duplicate-cross-repo.md`):

```python
body = templates_mod.render(tmpl, "close-duplicate-cross-repo", canonical_url=url)
return [
    {"kind": "comment", "body": body},
    {"kind": "close", "reason": "not planned"},
], None
```

The stated reason (Plan 4 executor design, and the comment in the code) is that GitHub's duplicate close is same-repo only.

## The question

**That premise was never verified.** It may be wrong — GitHub's UI does appear to allow marking an issue a duplicate of one in another repository, and the GraphQL `closeIssue` input takes a `duplicateIssueId` node ID, which is repo-agnostic on its face.

If `duplicateIssueId` does accept a cross-repo node ID, these closes could carry proper duplicate status instead of the weaker "not planned", which reads to a reporter as a decision not to act rather than a pointer to the live discussion.

## Work

1. **Verify empirically** whether `closeIssue(stateReason: DUPLICATE, duplicateIssueId: <node id in another repo>)` succeeds, using two scratch issues in two repos. This is the whole decision — everything below is contingent on it.
2. If it works: use the native duplicate close for cross-repo pairs too, and reword or retire `close-duplicate-cross-repo.md` accordingly (the reporter still benefits from being told the canonical lives elsewhere).
3. If it does not: leave the behaviour as-is and record the verified finding in a code comment, so the premise stops being folklore.

## Notes for whoever picks this up

- **No egress-guard change is needed either way.** `closeIssue` is already in both `ALLOWED_OPERATIONS` and `ALLOWED_MUTATION_FIELDS` (`src/triage_verse/gh.py:41`, `:54`), and `gh_mutation`'s declared-repo check takes the repo list explicitly — so a cross-repo duplicate close is already expressible without weakening the guard.
- `undo` already handles this path: `_reverse_mutations` reverses both `close` and `close-duplicate` with a `reopen` plus a `delete-comment`, so switching the mutation kind does not need an undo change.
- Only same-repo behaviour is currently covered by `test_close_duplicate_same_repo`; the cross-repo fallback is pinned by `test_close_duplicate_cross_repo_falls_back_to_not_planned`, which will need updating if the behaviour changes.

## Origin

Noticed while confirming that #15 ("close duplicate Issues on PR submission") was already implemented — see the closing comment there. The other gap noted in that comment, `cross_repo_option` being computed but never acted on, was fixed in #53.

title: review app: an approved suggest-transfer that never executes disappears from both the queue and the Transfers tab
description:
## Context

PR #53 added a **Transfers** tab: a worklist of approved `suggest-transfer` proposals awaiting a human to actually move the issue on GitHub. The whole reason it exists is stated in the design spec — approving a transfer suggestion applies a `wrong location` label but does not move anything, and approved proposals leave the review queue, so without a worklist "the judgement gets recorded and then lost".

`review_queue.pending_transfers` (`src/triage_verse/review_queue.py:258`) takes an optional `results_dir` and, when given, lists only suggestions whose label has actually been applied. The review app passes it.

That gating was added deliberately, to fix a race: `record_transferred` writes a later, terminal decision for the same proposal, and `executor.select_executable` only executes the *latest* decision per proposal. So marking a transfer done **before** `execute --apply` ran would silently cancel the label — whether the label landed depended purely on race order, with no results record explaining why.

## Problem

The gating reintroduces a narrower version of the failure the tab exists to prevent.

An approved `suggest-transfer` whose label was never applied now appears in **neither** surface:

- not in the **review queue** — `approved` is in `TERMINAL_VERDICTS`, so the proposal is done as far as the queue is concerned;
- not in the **Transfers tab** — no `applied` result, so `pending_transfers` filters it out.

Two ways to get there:

1. **`execute` errors on that decision.** `plan_decision` can legitimately return an error — e.g. the canonical is unparseable, the canonical's repo is the issue's own, or (new in #53) the canonical has no mirror row. That writes `status="error"`, which is in `FINAL_STATUSES`, so the decision is permanently consumed. Only `stale-needs-rereview` bounces a proposal back to the queue, so there is no path to re-review it.
2. **`execute --apply` simply never runs** for that batch, or runs in dry-run only.

Either way a reviewer's judgement is recorded and then invisible. It is strictly better than the label-cancelling bug it replaced — nothing wrong is written to GitHub — but it is not clean, and there's no signal anywhere in the UI that it happened.

## Suggested fix

Make the un-executed state **visible rather than filtered**. Options, roughly in order of preference:

- List approved-but-not-yet-applied suggestions in the Transfers tab with a distinct badge (e.g. "label pending") and **disable** the *Mark transferred* control for them — that preserves the race fix (you still cannot mark before the label lands) while keeping the item on screen.
- Additionally surface decisions whose latest result is `status="error"`, with the error text, so a `plan_decision` failure is actionable instead of silent. This is the more general gap: an errored decision is currently a dead end everywhere, not just for transfers.

## Related

The dead-end-on-error shape is pre-existing (it applies to the label-allowlist errors too), but #53 made it reachable from **mirror freshness** rather than only from decision content, which is a lower bar. Worth considering whether errored decisions deserve a general re-review path rather than a transfers-specific fix.

_Filed from review of #53._

title: sync: totalCount guard will chronically refuse reconciliation on busy repos
description:
## Context

PR #53 added sync-side reconciliation: on a **full** sync, `sync.reconcile_repo` deletes mirror rows for issues GitHub no longer lists, so a transferred issue's source row doesn't linger as a ghost. (The ghost is harmful — it pairs with its own transferred copy at cosine ~1.0 and dedup proposes closing the *live* issue as a duplicate of one that no longer exists.)

To avoid deleting live issues, the guard at `src/triage_verse/sync.py:140-147` refuses to retire anything when the walk saw fewer issues than GitHub's reported `totalCount`:

```python
if total_count is not None and len(seen) < total_count:
    log(f"  reconcile {repo}: REFUSING to retire anything -- the walk saw ...")
    return []
```

## Problem

That condition is likely to be true on **every** run for an active repo, not just occasionally.

`_walk_updated_desc` pages the issues connection ordered `UPDATED_AT DESC`. Any issue that receives a comment mid-walk jumps to the front of the ordering — a page already fetched — so it never enters `seen`. With `rstudio/shiny` at ~2,780 issues that's ~56 pages for issues alone (the whole repo is ~195 requests, minutes of wall time), so a single comment landing during the walk trips the guard.

Consequence: **reconciliation may effectively never run on the largest repos** — precisely the ones where transfers and ghost rows matter most. The direction is fail-safe (it deletes nothing and logs loudly, so this is a feature-doesn't-run outcome, never data loss), but the feature is silently inert where it's needed.

Note this only affects `sync --full`; incremental syncs never reconcile, by design.

## Suggested fix

Don't gate the whole repo on an exact count match. Instead verify only the **deletion candidates**, which are normally zero:

1. Compute `gone` as today (mirrored issues absent from `seen`).
2. For each candidate, do a confirmation read — `gh api repos/{repo}/issues/{n}` is an allowed read under the egress guard.
3. Delete only those GitHub confirms are absent. Check `repository_url` on the response to distinguish a genuinely-gone issue from a 301-followed **transfer** (a transferred issue's old number redirects to its new home, so a naive 200 would look like "still live").

That is strictly more precise than the count comparison, costs nothing in the common case (no candidates → no requests), and also closes the residual gap the count guard can't catch: a *partially truncated* response (page 1 returns, then a false `hasNextPage: false`) leaves `seen` non-empty and consistent with a lower count, so the current guard wouldn't fire.

Keep the existing zero-issues refusal at `sync.py:148+` as a cheap belt-and-braces check.

## Trigger

Worth doing before enabling `rstudio/shiny` or `posit-dev/py-shiny` in `config/repos.yaml` — see the SYNC POLICY note at the top of that file. Until then the active pilot is a ~30-request full sync where the race is unlikely.

_Filed from review of #53._

title: CLI: --json output mode on every command
description:
## Problem

The `triage-verse` CLI is human-first: status and results go to stdout as prose/tables, and structured interchange happens through files (`.data/proposals/`, decision JSONL, `analytics.json`). That works for the current workflow, but it makes the CLI awkward to compose — for scripts, for dashboards, and especially for coding agents, which are increasingly the thing driving it.

## Prior art

kata (katatracker.com) treats agents as the primary consumer and puts `--json` (plus a terser `--agent` mode) on **every** command as a global flag. Any command's outcome — list, create, sync result, status — is machine-readable without screen-scraping.

## Proposal

Add a global `--json` flag to the `triage-verse` CLI:

- Every command emits a single JSON document (or JSONL for list-like output) on stdout when the flag is set; human prose goes to stderr or is suppressed.
- Highest-value commands first: `sync` (per-repo counts/cursors), `analyze-status` (in-flight batches, spend), `verify-counts` (mismatches), `analytics export` already has a file target but should support stdout.
- Errors also structured (`{"error": ...}`) with nonzero exit codes preserved.

Incremental adoption is fine — a shared helper in `cli.py` plus per-command opt-in, rather than a big-bang rewrite.

title: P3 apply stage: credential egress guard for GitHub writes
description:
## Problem

Triage-verse runs LLM-generated proposals with `gh` credentials, and the future P3 apply stage will write to GitHub (labels, comments, closes). Today nothing structurally prevents a misfired prompt, a bug, or a compromised dependency from using that credential against the wrong repo, the wrong endpoint, or the wrong verb. The blast radius of "the prompt misfired" should be a log line, not an incident.

## Prior art

kata (katatracker.com) wraps its GitHub HTTP transport in an origin guard: credentials are only attached to requests whose URL matches the bound repo's API paths; everything else is refused before the request leaves the process. Notably, when we hit a bug in that guard (kenn-io/kata#168), it **failed closed** — it blocked a legitimate pagination request rather than ever risking sending the token elsewhere. That's the right failure mode for this class of tool. (Their bug — GitHub pagination `Link` headers use numeric `/repositories/{id}/...` URLs — is also a lesson for our allowlist: canonicalize URLs before matching.)

## Proposal

A thin guard layer that all GitHub **write** calls go through (reads via the mirror sync can adopt it later):

- **Repo allowlist:** only repos active in `config/repos.yaml`.
- **Endpoint/verb allowlist:** only the specific operations the apply stage supports (e.g. add/remove label, create comment, close issue) — deny by default, including anything org- or user-scoped.
- **Fail closed** with a clear error naming the refused URL/operation, and log every refusal.
- Enforced at the single choke point where requests are made (our `gh.py` wrapper), so new call sites can't bypass it accidentally.

## Notes

- This complements, not replaces, the human-review gate: it bounds what *approved-and-executing* actions can touch.
- Pairs with the single-external-writer invariant (only the designated apply stage may write to GitHub at all) — can be the same choke point.

title: decisions: record decided_by (actor) and optional reason on review decisions
description:
## Problem

Decision records (`src/triage_verse/decisions.py`) capture the proposal, verdict, and timestamp — but not **who** decided or **why**:

```python
{
    "id": ...,
    "proposal_id": ...,
    "repo": ..., "issue": ...,
    "action": ..., "params": ...,
    "verdict": verdict,
    "confidence": ...,
    "decided_at": ...,
}
```

Today that's tolerable because a single human reviews everything. But the program's trajectory is more automation and possibly more reviewers. When someone asks "why did this issue get closed as duplicate?" months from now, the decision log should answer with the actor (human username, or model + version for automated verdicts) and a short justification — not just `verdict: approve`.

This is the "audit-ready" idea from kata (katatracker.com): closing an issue there *requires* an explicit completion claim with evidence and actor attribution. Adopting the attribution half now is a small schema change; retrofitting it later is an archaeology problem.

## Proposal

- Add `decided_by` to every decision record. Default for the review app: the local GitHub login (`gh api user`) or `$USER`; automated pipelines record `model:<id>` (e.g. `model:claude-sonnet-5`).
- Add optional `reason` (free text). The review app can offer it on reject/edit verdicts where the "why" is least recoverable; approvals can leave it empty.
- Readers must tolerate old records missing both fields (JSONL is append-only; no migration).

## Out of scope

Evidence links (commit SHAs etc.) à la `kata close --commit` — not meaningful until the P3 apply stage writes back to GitHub; revisit then.

title: Plan 3e: Keyboard-driven review + edit action
description:
Parent: #9

Add keyboard-driven approve/reject/edit to the review queue (the master spec calls for keyboard-driven review; the 3a slice ships buttons only), plus an **edit** action to adjust a proposal's params before approving (e.g. change the proposed label/priority). Edit was deferred from 3a because it is low-value until there is enough evidence surface to know what a better value would be.

title: Plan 3d: Review close / close-duplicate proposals
description:
Parent: #9

Extend the review queue to the higher-stakes `close` and `close-duplicate` proposal action types (already emitted by the Plan 2 pipeline into the same proposals JSONL, currently filtered out of the queue by `review_queue.SUPPORTED_ACTIONS`).

Deferred deliberately until the issue/PR drawer (#32) exists, so a reviewer has full evidence — issue body, comment thread, and the duplicate's sibling issue — before approving a close.

title: Plan 3c: Dashboard tab
description:
Parent: #9

A dashboard tab in the review app: backlog burndown per repo, opened-vs-closed per week, close-reason mix, triage coverage, queue depth/throughput, per-category precision, and per-stage spend.

Deferred from the Plan 3a first slice. Note: most of the underlying series are already computed in `src/triage_verse/analytics.py` (currently unwired to any UI), so this is largely a UI task.

title: Plan 3b: Issue/PR slide-over drawer
description:
Parent: #9

A GitHub-Projects-style slide-over drawer that renders the full item from the mirror — title, body, comment thread, labels, state, linked evidence — anywhere an issue or PR appears (queue, dashboard, dupe pairs), with a deep link out to GitHub. Review should never require leaving the app.

Deferred from the Plan 3a first slice. Unblocks reviewing higher-stakes proposals (see 3d) by giving enough on-screen evidence to judge them.

title: Plan 3a: Review queue for label/priority proposals
description:
Parent: #9

First slice of the Plan 3 review app. A plain Shiny-for-Python queue for `add-label`/`set-priority` proposals: sorted by confidence descending, per-row Approve/Reject/Skip buttons, a bulk "Approve visible rows" action, decisions written to an append-only JSONL log, and filtering of already-decided proposals, out-of-scope action types, and issues no longer open in the mirror.

Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-01-plan-3-review-queue-design.md`
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-01-plan-3-review-queue.md`

Implemented in #28.

title: review queue: a malformed proposal id crashes the whole queue render, not just its row
description:
## Context
In the review-queue app (`src/triage_verse/review_app/app.py`, added in #28), each proposal's `id` is passed directly to Shiny's dynamic module namespace (`row_ui(row_id, ...)` / `row_server(row_id, ...)`). Shiny's `validate_id` only permits letters, numbers, and underscore in a namespace id.

## Problem
If any proposal `id` contains a character outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]` (e.g. a hyphen), the `@render.ui` `queue_ui` output raises `ValueError: The string '...' is not a valid id` during render — and because the whole queue is rendered in one `queue_ui` output, **one bad id blanks the entire queue**, not just that row. The page shows only the error, with no rows reviewable.

## Severity
Low / latent. Real proposal ids are generated as `uuid4().hex` (`src/triage_verse/proposals.py`), which is always namespace-safe, so this cannot happen with actual pipeline output. It only surfaced when hand-writing a demo fixture with a hyphenated id. Filing for robustness, not because it's currently reachable.

## Suggested fix
Make the render defensive so a single bad row degrades gracefully instead of taking down the queue. Options:
- Skip proposals whose `id` fails `shiny`'s id validation, logging a warning (consistent with how `review_queue._iter_jsonl_records` already skips malformed JSON lines); or
- Derive the module namespace from a sanitized/hashed id rather than the raw `id`, keeping the raw id only in the record; or
- Wrap per-row rendering so one row's failure renders an inline error for that row only.

Skipping-with-a-warning is the simplest and matches existing malformed-input handling in `review_queue.py`.

_Filed from review of #28 (Plan 3a review queue)._

title: review queue: rescan of all proposal/decision JSONL on every load won't scale
description:
## Context
The review-queue app (`src/triage_verse/review_queue.py`, added in #28) loads the queue by re-reading **every** `.jsonl` file under `.data/proposals/**` and `.data/decisions/**` on each call to `load_undecided` — parsing all lines, building a set of decided `proposal_id`s, and filtering. `load_undecided` runs on every app load and after every decision (approve/reject/skip/bulk-approve).

This was a deliberate choice for the first slice: at the current pilot scale (~10k total proposal + decision records) a full re-parse is milliseconds, and the design spec (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-01-plan-3-review-queue-design.md`, "Open items" #2) documents it as intentional, with this issue as the flagged follow-up.

## Problem
The cost is O(total records) per load, and it grows unbounded as decisions accumulate — the decisions log is append-only and never pruned. Once the full ~42-repo blitz is in scope (proposal/decision volume growing roughly an order of magnitude), re-scanning both trees on every decision could become a noticeable per-click delay.

## Suggested fix (when the trigger hits)
Either:
- **mtime-aware incremental scan** — cache parsed records per file, re-read only files whose mtime changed since the last scan; or
- **small SQLite index** of decided `proposal_id`s (and/or proposals), updated incrementally on write.

The log remains the source of truth in both cases; the index is derived and rebuildable.

## Trigger
Not worth doing now. Revisit when proposal/decision record count or file count grows ~10× (i.e. when the full fleet is being triaged), or if queue load latency becomes noticeable in practice.

_Filed from review of #28 (Plan 3a review queue)._

title: Initialize CLAUDE.md with project conventions (incl. 'lots of logging' preference)
description:
## Task

Initialize a `CLAUDE.md` file at the repo root with project-specific instructions for AI coding agents working in this codebase.

## Context

There's currently no `CLAUDE.md` in the repo. Barret wants one, and has an explicit preference to record now while it's fresh:

- **Prefers lots of logging.** In particular, long-running or multi-stage operations (like `triage-verse analyze`, which drives a resumable multi-stage state machine with an internal wait/poll loop) should log clearly at the start and end of every stage, plus a periodic heartbeat during any wait/retry loop — so it's never ambiguous whether a long run is progressing or stuck. This was added directly to `analyze.py` (see commit `a1bf876`); `CLAUDE.md` should capture it as a standing convention for future work in this codebase, not just a one-off fix.

## Suggested scope

- Standard `CLAUDE.md` sections: what the project is, how to run tests (`make py-check`), key entry points (`triage-verse` CLI), where config lives (`config/models.yaml`, `config/repos.yaml`).
- A logging-verbosity convention section capturing the preference above.
- Pointers to `docs/superpowers/specs/`, `docs/superpowers/plans/`, and `decisions/` and their purposes (design specs, implementation plans, durable architecture-decision records), including the house rule that specs/plans/decisions are historical records and should not be rewritten after the fact.

Barret said he'll write this himself — this issue exists to make sure it doesn't get lost, and to hand off the "lots of logging" preference as context for whoever (human or agent) ends up drafting it.

---
Related: #8 (Plan 2), #19 (worker pool — where the logging-visibility need first came up).

title: claude_cli: surviving 'submitted' batch row + process restart raises KeyError in results()
description:
## Problem

Discovered as an adjacent finding during the worker-pool feature's final review (PR #22) — this is **pre-existing** behavior from before that feature (present since commit `184a486`), not something the worker pool introduced or worsened.

`ClaudeCliClient` (the `claude_cli` backend) keeps its batch results **only in memory**: `self._batches: dict[str, list[BatchResult]]`, populated inside `submit()`. If a process is killed after `analyze._submit_stage` has committed a `batches` row with `status='submitted'` for a synchronous-client chunk, but *before* that chunk is collected in the same process, the `batches` row survives the crash — but the actual results it refers to do not (they lived only in the dead process's memory).

On restart, a **fresh** `ClaudeCliClient` instance is constructed with an empty `self._batches`. `analyze()`'s resume logic finds the surviving `submitted` row via `db.open_batches(...)` and adopts that run rather than starting a new one (correct instinct — it thinks there's in-flight work to collect). But when it then calls `client.results(provider_batch_id)` on the *new* instance, `self._batches[provider_batch_id]` raises `KeyError`, since this instance never populated that key.

## Why this hasn't surfaced yet

Since the per-item persistence fix (#21/#23) and the worker-pool feature, both the sequential-synchronous path (chunk size 1) and the parallel path insert `batches` rows and immediately collect them within the *same* function call, before returning — so in normal operation there is no window where a `submitted` row survives across a process boundary for the `claude_cli` backend. The gap is a race between "committed the `batches` insert" and "collected it," which is narrow but real: a kill in that exact window reproduces it.

## Fix options

- Detect this case explicitly: if `client.status(...)`/`client.results(...)` can't find a provider_batch_id it doesn't recognize, treat the batch as unrecoverable and re-queue its items instead of raising — since the underlying work was never actually completed from this process's perspective anyway (it's synchronous, so "submitted but this instance doesn't know it" effectively means "never really executed by this process").
- Or: never leave the window open at all — always insert-and-collect a synchronous batch inside one uninterruptible sequence (already true for the steady-state per-item and per-worker-item paths; only the initial `db.insert_batch`/`commit` step before `_try_collect_batch`/`_record_and_apply` runs is the narrow window).

## Scope

Low priority — the window is narrow (between one `commit()` and the next few lines of code in the same function) and this only matters for a crash landing in that exact spot. Not a merge blocker for any current work; tracked for whenever the `claude_cli` backend's crash-resilience gets more attention (see also #21, #23, #24).

---
Related: #8 (Plan 2), #19 (parallelize — where this was discovered as an adjacent finding), #21, #23 (durability fixes that narrowed but didn't close this exact window).

title: claude_cli: back off on rate-limit failures instead of burning the content-retry budget
description:
## Context

Issue #19 (parallelize `claude -p` calls with a bounded worker pool) increases the chance of hitting Claude Code's own subscription rate limits, since multiple `claude -p` subprocesses will run concurrently against the same account instead of one at a time.

## Problem

`ClaudeCliClient.submit_one` currently treats every failure the same way: a non-zero exit or a runner exception counts as one failed attempt toward its existing 2-attempt retry budget, then the item is marked `errored` and skipped (to be picked up again on a future `analyze` run, since results are cached by content hash). This is fine for the sequential path where failures are rare and independent, but a rate-limit response is a *predictable, load-driven* failure, not a random one — under N concurrent workers, hitting a rate limit is likely to affect several in-flight items at once, and immediately burning the 2-attempt budget on a "try again in a few seconds" condition wastes both attempts (and the spend already incurred on them) for no benefit.

## Proposal

Detect a rate-limit-flavored failure specifically (distinguishable exit code, stderr pattern, or `is_error`/`api_error_status` field in the CLI's JSON envelope — needs checking against real `claude -p` output under load) and handle it differently from a generic failure:
- Back off (e.g. a short sleep, possibly with jitter across workers to avoid a thundering herd) and retry, without consuming the item's normal 2-attempt content-quality retry budget.
- Consider a global backoff signal shared across workers (e.g. if one worker hits a rate limit, briefly pause new dispatches from the pool) rather than each worker independently retrying blind.

## Scope

Deferred and out of scope for the initial worker-pool implementation (#19) — the pool ships first with N=2 (a small, conservative worker count unlikely to aggressively trip rate limits immediately), and this refinement follows once real usage shows how the CLI actually behaves under concurrent load.

---
Related: #19 (parallelize claude -p), #8 (Plan 2).

title: claude_cli: a crash/kill mid-stage loses all in-flight spend (no incremental persistence)
description:
## Problem

Under the `claude_cli` backend, a stage's results are held **only in memory** until the whole stage finishes. `ClaudeCliClient.submit()` loops over every item in a chunk sequentially and returns only after all of them are done; `analyze._submit_stage` writes anything to the database (`batches`, `batch_items`, and — after `_collect` runs — `classifications`/`dedup_verdicts`/`spend`) only *after* that `client.submit(chunk)` call returns:

```python
provider_id = client.submit(chunk)          # blocks until every item in the chunk is done
db.insert_batch(con, batch_id, run_id, stage, provider_id, len(chunk))
db.insert_batch_items(con, batch_id, ...)
con.commit()
```

If the process is interrupted — killed, crashes, machine reboots, OOM — **while still inside that `client.submit(chunk)` call**, none of the already-completed (and already-paid-for) items in that chunk are recorded anywhere. A restart sees no `batches` row for the stage, treats it as never-started, and re-selects the same issues for (re-)processing — paying again for every item, not just the ones that hadn't run yet.

This is distinct from and more severe than #21 (the `max_usd_per_day` breaker not being checked mid-stage): #21 is about a safety *limit* not applying mid-stage; this is about *durability* — even with no budget concern at all, any interruption mid-stage discards that stage's entire progress with no partial credit and no way to know which items were already done.

## Impact

- At pilot scale (tens of issues) this is a minor annoyance.
- At fleet scale (thousands of issues per stage across ~40 repos), any interruption during a long-running classify/recheck/dedup stage means total loss of that stage's spend to that point, with a full re-pay required on restart. Long unattended runs are exactly where interruptions (crashes, reboots, OOM) become likely.
- `analyze()`'s existing resume logic (adopting an in-flight `run_id`, `_stage_started` guards against resubmission) only protects *already-committed* stages — it does nothing here, because nothing was committed yet.

## Fix options

1. **Cheapest, no interface change:** chunk `claude_cli` submissions at a much smaller granularity than `max_requests_per_batch` (down to 1 item per chunk). Since `_submit_stage` already persists `batches`/`batch_items` after every `client.submit(chunk)` call, a chunk size of 1 means every single item is durably recorded before the next one starts — a kill between any two items loses at most the one in-flight call, never a whole stage. This uses existing machinery; it only requires the `claude_cli` path to pick a small chunk size (independent of the `max_requests_per_batch` used for `anthropic_batch`, where large chunks make sense since that backend doesn't run items synchronously).
2. **More general:** give `ClaudeCliClient.submit()` (or `BatchClient.submit()` generally) an optional per-item completion callback, so `analyze.py` can persist each result to the database as it lands, regardless of chunk size.

Option 1 is the simplest fix and directly usable today; option 2 is the more architecturally clean long-term answer if other backends ever need the same incremental-persistence property.

---
Related: #8 (Plan 2), #18 (Batch API backend), #19 (parallelize), #21 (breaker granularity — a safety-limit sibling of this durability issue).

title: claude_cli: enforce max_usd_per_day within a stage (breaker bounds between runs, not within)
description:
## Problem

The analysis pipeline's `max_usd_per_day` circuit breaker is checked between chunks/stages in `analyze._submit_stage`, reading accumulated spend from the `spend` table. That works for the Batch API backend (`submit` is a cheap enqueue; cost is realized and recorded later during `_collect`). But the `claude_cli` backend (#18) incurs **all** real spend synchronously inside `ClaudeCliClient.submit()`, while spend is only written later in `_collect()`. So within a single stage the breaker never sees the in-flight spend: a stage of N issues fully executes and bills before the breaker can trip.

Net: under `claude_cli`, `max_usd_per_day` bounds spend **between stages/runs**, not **within a stage**.

## Impact

- Bounded but real cost-runaway exposure at fleet scale (a large repo's classify stage ≈ issues × ~$0.01–0.02 bills before any check).
- Invisible at pilot scale — the validated smoke run was 5 issues, $0.069.
- **Interim mitigation (already shipped):** documented in README / `config/models.yaml` / the `ClaudeCliClient` docstring; operators use `--limit` to bound a single run's spend.

## Fix options

- Interleave `_collect` (spend recording) per chunk inside `_submit_stage`, with a small `max_requests_per_batch` for `claude_cli`, so the between-chunk breaker check sees accumulating spend. This is backend-agnostic: a just-submitted *async* batch isn't `ended` yet, so `_collect` skips it and it's collected later as today.
- Or make `ClaudeCliClient` budget-aware: record spend incrementally and stop when a passed-in per-run budget is exceeded.
- Largely **moot under `anthropic_batch`** (#18), where cost is realized during polling as designed — so this only matters while `claude_cli` runs at scale.

---
Related: #8 (Plan 2), #18 (Batch API backend), #19 (parallelize).

title: feat(db): retain decision history via append-only classifications and dedup verdicts
description:
## Goal

The live SQLite DB should be the *complete* record for all analytics reports, so we never have to archive or post historical DB snapshots to GitHub. Today it's a "current state" DB: `classifications` and `dedup_verdicts` **upsert in place**, so each analysis run overwrites the prior verdict. To answer "what did it decide last week / in the previous run," you'd need an old DB file — which is exactly what we want to avoid.

This issue converts the two **decision tables** to append-only history so prior state, and *when/why it changed*, stay queryable in one DB.

Scope is intentionally limited to decision tables. Operational/batch state (`batches.status`) is **not** in scope — `runs`, `spend`, and existing batch timestamps already cover operational questions.

## Current behavior

- `classifications` — PK `(repo, number)`; `store()` upserts (`src/triage_verse/classify.py:157-186`).
- `dedup_verdicts` — PK `(repo_a, number_a, repo_b, number_b)`; `store()` upserts (`src/triage_verse/dedup.py:90-113`).
- Both already carry `run_id`, `at`, `model` (and `clf_hash` / `hash_a` / `hash_b`) — everything needed to attribute a change to a run and moment in time. The only thing forcing overwrite is the primary key.

## Proposed change

1. **Append instead of upsert.** Widen the PK to include `run_id` so each run's verdict is a new row. `store()` inserts a new row per run instead of `ON CONFLICT ... UPDATE`.
2. **Add "latest" views** — `classifications_latest` and `dedup_verdicts_latest` — that select the most recent row per key (by `at` / `run_id`). Existing read paths switch to these views so behavior is unchanged:
   - `proposals.build()` → reads latest.
   - recheck/skip logic that reads current classification + `clf_hash` → reads latest.
   - `analyze-status` and any status queries → reads latest.
3. **Migration.** Changing a PK in SQLite requires a table rebuild. Existing rows become the first history entry per key. Provide a migration that rebuilds the two tables with the new PK and preserves current rows.

## Out of scope

- Batch/run operational transition log (would be a separate issue only if a report needs batch turnaround / retry metrics).
- Full event-sourcing of all tables.

## Acceptance criteria

- Re-running analysis on an already-classified issue produces a **new** row rather than overwriting; the prior row remains.
- `*_latest` views return exactly one row per key, matching pre-change behavior.
- All existing read paths use the latest views; existing tests pass.
- A query can retrieve the full verdict history for a given issue / pair (prior states + `at` + `run_id` + `model`).
- Migration preserves existing verdicts.

title: Parallelize claude -p analysis calls to cut wall-clock time
description:
## Context

The `claude_cli` model backend (#18) runs one `claude -p` subprocess per issue, **sequentially**. Each call is a full agent turn — a trivial call measured ~2.7s; real classifications (rubric + issue body + comment thread) will be longer, an estimated ~5–15s each. That's fine for the pilot (`rstudio/shinytest2`, ~59 issues) but slow at scale.

## Problem

The full blitz is ~4,200 open issues × (Haiku classify + Sonnet recheck for low-confidence/close-candidates + Sonnet dedup adjudication per candidate pair) ≈ tens of thousands of sequential calls. At ~10s each, sequential wall-clock is **many hours to days**.

## Proposal

Run `claude -p` calls concurrently via a bounded worker pool inside `ClaudeCliClient.submit()`:

- Configurable concurrency (e.g. `claude_cli.concurrency: N` in `config/models.yaml`).
- Backoff + retry on rate-limit (HTTP 429 / usage-limit) responses — subscription auth is rate-limited, so concurrency must be *tuned*, not maxed.
- Preserve per-call spend capture (`total_cost_usd`) and the existing between-chunk `max_usd_per_day` circuit-breaker semantics.

## Expected impact

- **Time:** roughly N× wall-clock reduction, rate limits permitting — e.g. ~8–10× with modest concurrency turns days into hours.
- **Money:** no direct saving — same number of calls and tokens; this is throughput only.
- **Caveat:** largely **moot if a Console API key lands** (#18), because the Batch API is inherently async/bulk. So this is worth building only if `claude_cli` has to run at scale during the interim.

---
Related: #8 (Plan 2), #18 (Batch API backend).

title: Switch analysis pipeline to Anthropic Batch API once a Console API key is available
description:
## Situation

The Plan 2 analysis pipeline (#8) supports two model backends behind a single `BatchClient` interface, selected by `backend:` in `config/models.yaml`:

- **`anthropic_batch`** — Anthropic Message Batches API via the `anthropic` SDK. Requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (an Anthropic **Console / Developer Platform** key). 50% batch discount, async bulk throughput, per-token metered spend. **This is the preferred backend.**
- **`claude_cli`** — runs `claude -p --output-format json` on Claude Code's ambient auth (the enterprise subscription). No API key required. **This is what we use today.**

We currently have **no Console API key** — only Claude Enterprise / Claude Desktop, which are end-user products and do not issue API keys. Getting one is not self-serve; it needs the org's Anthropic **Developer Platform** access to be provisioned. Until then, `anthropic_batch` is unusable, and the `claude_cli` backend unblocks the pilot on credentials we actually have.

## Why the API key is the better path

A single trivial Haiku classification through `claude -p` measured **$0.0188** — almost entirely from ~19k tokens of Claude Code's *own* system prompt carried on every invocation (8.5k cache-create + 10.9k cache-read), plus we lose our shared-rubric prompt cache (each `claude -p` call is a fresh process).

| | Batch API (`anthropic_batch`) | CLI (`claude_cli`) |
|---|---|---|
| Discount | 50% batch | none |
| Per-call overhead | one shared, cached rubric prefix | ~19k Claude-Code system tokens **per call** |
| Throughput | async, bulk (up to 100k/batch) | 1 subprocess per issue, sequential |
| Spend control | per-token USD meter + `max_usd_per_day` | reported `total_cost_usd`; subscription rate limits |
| Structured output | `output_config` json_schema (guaranteed) | parse `result`, strip ``` fences, validate + retry |

Rough cost for the full ~4,200-issue blitz: the design estimate is **~$50–100 one-time** on Batch. Via `claude -p`, the overhead-dominated per-call cost (~$0.02+ each, across classify + recheck + dedup calls) is plausibly **several× that** and dramatically slower. (Only the single-call figure is measured; the blitz numbers are estimates.)

## Action

When the org provisions Anthropic Developer Platform / enterprise API access:
1. Create a Console API key.
2. Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `backend: anthropic_batch` in `config/models.yaml`.

The batch code path is already built and tested (`AnthropicBatchClient`), so this is a config flip — no new implementation needed.

---
Related: #8 (Plan 2). Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-29-plan-2-analysis-pipeline-design.md`.

title: CI is skipped for pull requests from maintainers with private org membership
description:
## Summary

The `tests` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is **skipped on every `pull_request` event**, even for maintainers, while `push` events to `main` run fine.

## Root cause

The job `if` gate requires `github.event.pull_request.author_association` to be `OWNER` or `MEMBER`:

```yaml
contains(fromJSON('["OWNER","MEMBER"]'), github.event.pull_request.author_association)
```

The `author_association` field in the **webhook payload** only reflects *public* org membership. A maintainer with **private** org membership is reported as `COLLABORATOR`/`CONTRIBUTOR` instead of `MEMBER`, so the allowlist skips their PR runs.

Verified for `@schloerke`:
- Repo permission: `admin`
- `GET /orgs/posit-dev/public_members/schloerke` → 404 (not a *public* member)
- `GET /orgs/posit-dev/members/schloerke` → 200 (is a member, privately)

The REST API reports `MEMBER` only because that call is authenticated as the user; the unauthenticated webhook payload does not.

## Fix

Drop the `author_association` allowlist and rely on the existing same-repo check, which is the real trust boundary:

```yaml
github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
```

A PR branch can only exist in this repo if its author has **write access** — outside contributors must fork, which fails this check. So forks and untrusted PRs remain blocked, while maintainers (regardless of membership visibility) are no longer skipped.

## Evidence

Recent PR runs all show `skipped`; `push` runs to `main` show `success`.

title: [aw] Detection Runs
description:
This issue tracks all runs where threat detection flagged problems in agentic workflows in this repository. Each workflow run that completes with a detection warning or failure posts a comment here.

<details>
<summary>What is a Detection Problem?</summary>

A detection problem occurs when the threat detection system either:
- **Detects potential security threats** (prompt injection, secret leak, malicious patch)
- **Fails to produce results** (agent failure, parse error)

When `continue-on-error: true` (the default), these problems produce warnings and safe outputs still proceed. When `continue-on-error: false`, they block safe outputs entirely.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How This Helps</summary>

This issue helps you:
- Track workflows where threat detection raised concerns
- Review patterns of detection warnings or failures
- Identify false positives or recurring issues with threat detection
- Monitor the health of the threat detection system

</details>

<details>
<summary>Resources</summary>

- [GitHub Agentic Workflows Documentation](https://github.com/github/gh-aw)

</details>

> [!TIP]
> To configure threat detection behavior, update the frontmatter:
> ```yaml
> safe-outputs:
>   threat-detection:
>     continue-on-error: true   # Warnings only (default)
>     # continue-on-error: false  # Strict mode — block safe outputs
> ```
